The Estate · Neo-Georgian

Then the house appears.

Ordered by Walter Hines Page in 1913. Completed by Leonard Tufts' craftsmen in 1916. Flemish bond brick. A brick water table at the foundation. White portico. Paired chimneys. A circular lawn held before the entrance like a pause.

Some houses hold history. This one shaped it.

Garran Hill · 1916

The door has been open
since 1916.

Neo-Georgian. Four columns. Original 1916 brick — three months were spent sourcing period-accurate replacements when restoration began. Seven fireplaces. 4.15 acres inside the Pinehurst ETJ. Six thousand and seventy-two square feet of living area.

Built by Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen. The same men who built Pinehurst.

A house this considered does not happen by accident. It begins with the man who ordered it.

Walter Hines Page · László portrait · London, 1917

The History · Walter Hines Page

He named it Garran Hill.
He never spent a night here.

Walter Hines Page bought the land in February 1913 and named it Garran Hill. Six weeks later, Woodrow Wilson appointed him Ambassador to the Court of St. James. He sailed for London into the First World War.

The house was completed without him. He served through the armistice. In December 1918, he came home — carried from the train at Aberdeen, mere miles from his land. He died ten days later.

From London, through four years of war, he wrote home constantly. He called it the farm.

"The farm — the farm — the farm."

The Life and Letters of Walter H. Page · Vol. I, P. 354 · 1923

He co-founded Doubleday, Page & Co. He edited The Atlantic Monthly. He nominated Woodrow Wilson for the presidency. Construction was supervised by his son Ralph. The craftsmen came from Leonard Tufts' crew — the same men building Pinehurst two miles away.

He never spent a night here.
"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"
Walter Hines Page  ·  Aberdeen, NC  ·  December 1918
He died ten days later.
The Threshold

The road carries the later name.
The threshold keeps the first.

The door has been open since 1916.

Original leaded glass sidelights. Herringbone brick underfoot. Original hardware on every solid-wood door. White raised-panel wainscoting to chair rail.

GARRAN HILL · 1916 — inlaid in the brick before ground was broken.

The staircase — mahogany volute — has turned the same curve since 1916.

→ Begin the 3D Tour
The stair was redrawn from newel to cornice. Nothing was approximated.
The Salon

They made it bigger
so they could dance.

The salon runs nearly forty feet. Tall bare windows parade down both sides. One end anchored by a fireplace. Coffered ceiling. Seven carved mantels saved from the original structure, repaired and reset.

It is a room that expects people in it.

The Drawing Room

Fire going.
No one home yet.

Georgian carved mantel. Delft tile surround — blue and white, hand-painted, original. The arch motif that runs through the entire house appears here in the cabinetry, in the doorways, in the fanlights above.

It was specified in 1916. It is still there.

The Dining Room

The shell cabinets were already there
in 1916.

Original frontpiece. Shell cabinets — still there. Butler's arched niche. The room holds its proportions: 17 feet by 19. It has not been asked to be something else.

The Library

Not original.
Deliberate.

Built-in shelving on three walls. Floor to ceiling. Rolling ladder. French doors to the rear grounds. Brass chandelier. Designed in 2000 to the same standard as the 1916 house it joined.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

The Kitchen

White cabinetry. Dark granite. Island.
Four windows.

The kitchen was not updated. It was designed. Reclaimed heart-pine floors — the only room in the house that departs from the original oak. Two farm sinks. Custom island. The wall of windows faces an expanse of grass bordered by elder magnolias.

Every morning at 6:30, the deer come through.

The shell cabinets are original. The kitchen is not. Both are right.
The Primary Suite

Designed from scratch in 2000
to match 1916 proportions.

Custom wall panels. A fireplace with a full mantel drawing. Shower walls drawn at full tile detail. Every component specified — not selected from a catalogue.

Fifteen architectural drawings document the decisions Thomas O'Shea made. They survive. They transfer with the property.

The primary balcony — 24 by 11 feet — faces the grounds.

The Powder Room
Fuchsia chinoiserie.
Tennessee marble.

The arch motif — consistent through every door since 1916. The brass hardware, original.

4.15 Acres · Private Grounds

The world outside these gates
does not exist here.

Low-voltage landscape lighting along the entry drive. Underground utilities throughout. Twenty-eight irrigation zones fed by a 130-foot well. A 20-by-40-foot salt water pool, surrounded by a brick wall with iron gates. Restored in 2022.

The Wee Cottage — complete, self-contained — was moved to the grounds by sky crane.

In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest.
Someone still puts flowers there.
Blue Fox  ·  Betty Dumaine's Irish Hunter  ·  Buried on the Grounds
1959 – 1984

Some places remember
who loved them.

Elizabeth Dumaine purchased the property in 1959. She was a foxhunter. She added stables, kennels, and an enclosure for peacocks — known to be guard birds. She changed the name to Hollycrest. She hosted royalty.

Her favorite horse is buried on the grounds.

Blue Fox. Someone still puts flowers there.

The Restoration · 1999–2001

Beauty was not enough.
The house needed discipline.

In 1999 a Durham architect, Thomas O'Shea, drew the house from scratch — every room measured, every cornice profiled, every proportion committed to paper before a single board was replaced. Contractor Dennis Dunagan spent three years executing those drawings. What stands today is what was designed.

All seven carved mantels saved. Most of the original oak flooring lifted, repaired, and relaid. The period-accurate portico brick took three months to source. Custom Marvin windows made to match the 1916 originals. A five-zone climate system engineered to protect the original architecture.

Fifteen architectural drawings survive. They transfer with the property.

It does not feel added. It feels inevitable.

Preservation · National Register

Every claim is sourced.
Every fact is verified.

The Pines Preservation Guild visited in April 2024. The property qualifies under Criterion B — associated with individuals making significant contributions to history.

A preservation easement is available: North Carolina tax credit of 25% of fair market value, up to $500,000. Federal income tax deduction potential. A candidate for the National Register.
